cards.title: RCS vs SMS/MMS: what changes in the message
cards.summary: RCS is a distinct messaging protocol with SMS fallback that upgrades text-only or single-image messages into rich carousels, video, web views and native action buttons.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pilot RCS for campaign sends or transactional/drop messaging, and scoping which message formats to build for it.
steps: Understand RCS as a separate protocol from SMS/MMS, not a formatting tweak: SMS is text-only, MMS adds an image, RCS supports carousels, scrolling, video and embedded web views inside the messaging thread. Where a recipient can't receive RCS, the message falls back to SMS, so keep an SMS-safe version of every send.

Exploit native phone integrations for commerce use cases: action buttons can be programmed as any CTA, and calendar functionality lets a pre-launch drop message offer 'add to calendar' instead of 'watch this space' — replacing a reminder prompt with an actual saved event.
Know that consumers are already trained on this interaction pattern (iMessage-style rich bubbles have existed for years), so richer messages don't require teaching the customer new behavior.
Treat RCS as an early-adopter inbox-distinction play: the present lift partly comes from standing out versus SMS-only brands, and the source expects that advantage to diminish as adoption grows.
Weigh the cost: RCS is somewhat more expensive than SMS because carriers take a cut, so a pilot should be judged on incremental performance, not just message-level cost.
caveats: The source's claim of outsized RCS performance over SMS/MMS is a current observation from one provider and its brand base, not a benchmark; the source itself names carrier cost/performance as the main threat to the channel.
RCS availability details vary and change quickly — verify current device and carrier coverage before planning a send.
Live brand example mentioned: one brand switched to RCS with a holdout group running to measure incremental impact.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Test RCS by holding out or running a clean flow
cards.summary: Operationalize an RCS switch with either a holdout group for incremental read or a deliberately simple one-to-one flow for a cleaner test signal.
cards.use_when: Launching or planning a first RCS campaign and needing to decide how to structure the test so results are trustworthy.
steps: Choose your measurement design up front. One option discussed: run a holdout so you can read the incremental impact of the new RCS experience versus the baseline SMS path. The other option: keep the RCS flow deliberately one-to-one and simple first, then test richer elements (carousels, cards) so the effect of each addition is cleaner.
If you change flow and format at the same time, you can't attribute lift to RCS versus your new creative — separate the protocol change from the creative change where possible.
Only after a clean baseline read should you layer richer formats: carousels for recommendations, web views for expanded browsing, action buttons for CTAs.
Build the SMS fallback version of each RCS send so the holdout/control experience is a true comparison, not a broken message.
caveats: The source only states this as an intended approach ('we'll probably go a little bit more one to one and then we'll test to get a cleaner read') — it is a plan, not a proven result.
Early-adopter novelty effects can inflate RCS lift; expect the advantage to shrink as more brands adopt the channel.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Conversational carousels for product recommendation
cards.summary: Use RCS carousels inside a conversational thread to answer 'what do you recommend' with a small set of tailored best-sellers plus a native web view.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and PDP/landing-page substitution inside SMS/RCS: when a customer asks for a recommendation and you need to move them to a purchase path in-thread.
steps: Treat the conversational recommendation as a replacement for sending bare links. Where the old flow produced a few links in reply to 'I'm buying for a guy who likes the outdoors — what do you recommend?', the richer flow returns a carousel of three items curated for that buyer type.
Constrain the carousel to a small, opinionated set (the source uses three) so the customer makes a choice rather than browsing a catalog in a text thread.
Lean on attached web view so the customer can expand into a native browser experience inside the messaging app — the whole browse-to-buy path stays in the thread.
Use the carousel to serve best-seller logic for a persona/use-case rather than one generic product, and feed objection data from these conversations back into your other flows.
Because the format relies on consumer familiarity with in-thread rich content, no new customer education is needed; the constraint is building the recommendation logic behind it.
caveats: The recommendation-carousel capability is described as a future/planned application by the source, not a documented live result.
Named brand (Ridge) is used illustratively — do not treat it as evidence of conversion lift.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: List growth first: fix pop-up opt-in rate
cards.summary: For a $5–10M brand trying to grow SMS, the highest-leverage first move is on-site opt-in rate, because list size is the top of the funnel for every downstream send.
cards.use_when: Auditing SMS as an acquisition/growth channel and deciding where to spend first effort on list growth.
steps: Start with on-site opt-in. The source names it the fastest way to grow an SMS list, ahead of other capture methods, because it sits at the very top of your own-channel funnel and pays off in every future campaign.
If you do nothing else, fix the pop-up acquisition rate first — treat it as the single most important list-growth lever before adding new flows or formats.
Add fun/compelling content to the pop-up to lift opt-in rate; one brand explicitly says they had been under-optimizing pop-ups and are now doing it aggressively.
Make this an owned-site-team responsibility: the source recommends having your site team drive the opt-in effort aggressively and watch that the metric trends up.

Recognize the strategic logic: more numbers means more people you can text, and the source long considered list-growth capability the main differentiator between SMS providers (now shifting toward features like conversational commerce and RCS).
caveats: The $5–10M annual revenue band is the source's own framing for who should prioritize this, not a universal threshold.
The claim that on-site opt-in is 'the best' capture method is the source's opinion, stated alongside acknowledgement that other methods exist.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Raise send cadence until unsubscribe rate ticks up
cards.summary: Increase message frequency one send at a time and let unsubscribe rate find your new ceiling, then treat that as the baseline.
cards.use_when: Setting campaign cadence for an established SMS program and deciding how many sends per week the list can absorb.
steps: Starting from your current cadence, add one more message per week (or one every two weeks if you send infrequently) as an increment, not a one-time jump.
Measure the unsubscribe rate after each increment and keep pushing until you see the unsubscribe rate begin to tick up — that inflection is where you stop and reset the baseline.
Do not treat the send-frequency question as separate from revenue: the point is to see how the added sends affect overall revenue from the channel, so track channel revenue alongside unsubscribes.
Once you find the ceiling, hold that cadence as your new baseline rather than reverting to the old, more conservative one.
Repeat the exercise periodically, since list composition and tolerance shift over time.
caveats: This is the source's recommended operating heuristic, not a measured benchmark; the correct ceiling differs by list and offer.
Pushing cadence without watching unsubscribe (and other list-health signals) can degrade the channel — the source explicitly uses unsub rate as the stop signal.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Ask customers why they didn't buy to feed all flows
cards.summary: Run conversational questions to surface purchase objections, then push that learning into your team and every flow — not just to generate incremental revenue.
cards.use_when: Running conversational SMS and using customer-research output to improve abandoned-cart, win-back, PDP and objection-handling flows.
steps: Start a conversational thread that asks questions rather than only pushing offers; the goal is to learn why people aren't purchasing, not solely to drive a sale in the thread.

Capture the objection reasons as customer insight and route them into the team's decision-making as fast as possible — the source treats asking customers directly as the fastest way to get this data into the team's head.
Apply the objections to your existing flows: if the recurring objection is shipping, sizing, price or trust, adjust the flow copy/offer that handles that stage.
Use the same mechanism to feed conversational recommendation logic (e.g., carousels of best-sellers for a stated use case) once you know the buyer intents coming in.
Run this before/alongside cadence expansion so you know what to say when you add sends.
caveats: The source frames conversational questions as valuable mainly for objection insight and revenue; it does not supply benchmarks or expected response rates.
If you use an AI 'shopper' assistant for conversational replies (the source's provider offers one), verify current capability and QA the answers before scaling.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Capture experiment learnings causally so the model earns trust
cards.summary: Operationalizing incrementality means running geo-lift and causal experiments and feeding them into your measurement model, so channel decisions are informed by tested lift rather than a black box.
cards.use_when: Attributing and budgeting across SMS/email/paid channels where you need to know which sends add incremental revenue versus cannibalize.
steps: Run structured experiments — the source uses a platform for all experiments and geo-lift testing — rather than inferring incrementality from last-click channel revenue.

Feed causal experiment results into your measurement mix model so the model is calibrated on tested lift; the source specifically values having experiments inform the MM ('causal MM') so it isn't a black box.
Use the resulting incrementality read to set the channel roadmap and budget, not just to report on past performance.
Apply the same framework to media mix and SMS sends so cadence and format decisions rest on observed lift rather than raw attributed revenue.
Build the muscle to distinguish lead conversion, purchase conversion and lift in this context before acting on the numbers.
caveats: This appears inside a sponsorship segment for a causal-MM vendor; treat the tool endorsement as promotional and evaluate measurement tools independently.
Causal-MM methodology and availability change — verify current product behavior before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Tactical SMS starting order for a mid-size brand
cards.summary: The source's recommended sequence for a $5–10M brand under-using SMS: fix pop-up opt-in, then expand cadence until unsubs rise, then add conversational questions.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing the first 30–90 days of an SMS improvement program when the team is lean and everything feels urgent.
steps: Step 1 — List growth: maximize subscribers through the on-site opt-in/pop-up and fix its acquisition rate first; this is the top of your owned-channel funnel and pays off later.
Step 2 — Cadence: add one send per interval and monitor unsubscribe rate, resetting your baseline at the point unsubs start rising; watch total channel revenue with it.
Step 3 — Conversation: begin asking customers questions to learn objections and purchase intent, and route those insights into all your flows.

Step 4 — Tooling/partner: if the team is lean and cannot execute the above, the source's own advice is to pick a hands-on platform that will push you toward the latest capabilities, accepting that this is the presenter's commercial pitch.
Sequence matters: list size and opt-in rate bound what cadence and conversation can deliver, so don't start by adding formats if your capture is weak.
caveats: The $5–10M band is the presenter's segmentation; smaller and larger brands may need a different order.
Step 4 is a vendor recommendation from the vendor's own employee and should not be read as an independent assessment.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx

cards.title: Checklist cadence: SMS/retention program for a growing brand
cards.summary: Small ecommerce teams run everything interconnected and hourly, so list health, cadence and message content should be managed as one operating rhythm.
cards.use_when: Running the day-to-day SMS/email lifecycle for a small ecom team and setting the review rhythm for list, cadence and messaging.
steps: Treat SMS/retention as small-team, high-frequency work: the source frames ecom as small teams doing big numbers where every hour matters and list, cadence and content are interconnected, so avoid optimizing one in isolation.
Keep a standing check on three top-of-funnel metrics together: pop-up opt-in rate (list growth), unsubscribe rate (list health), and channel revenue (output).
Change one lever at a time — a cadence increment or a format change — so you can tell what moved the unsubscribe rate.
Feed conversational objections back into the flows on a regular loop so the talking points stay current with what customers actually say.
Assign ownership: the source recommends the site team drive pop-up capture aggressively and watch the trend.
caveats: This is a synthesis of the source's advice rather than a single prescribed process.
Cadence and ceiling differ by list; no universal numeric target is established in the source.
cards.source_name: Rethinking SMS Marketing for Ecommerce_ AI, RCS & LTV.docx
